Participants viewed emotional and neutral images under natural viewing, reappraisal, expressive suppression, and baseline viewing instructions.

spans.text: The three other INST constituted the main experimental design and included emotional images only.

description.value: Neutral-image control condition. Participants judged the photographic quality of each neutral image, indicating whether it was well focused or properly lit, using a four-point button response. Images included either humans or inanimate settings and landscapes.

spans.text: The first INST served a control baseline (BASE), and was introduced to the participants as “a photographic quality” judgment

description.value: Natural or spontaneous emotion-experience condition. Participants watched emotional images and evaluated the depicted scenarios as if they corresponded to real situations to which they were personally exposed, then rated the feeling evoked by each image.

spans.text: To assess brain responses during “natural” or spontaneous emotion experience (NAT), participants were asked to watch and evaluate the depicted emotional scenarios as if they corresponded to real situations to which the participants would be personally exposed.

description.value: Cognitive reappraisal condition. Participants viewed emotional scenes as parts of a movie clip or television show displaying fake or artificially staged situations, with the aim of down-regulating emotional reactions, then rated the feeling evoked.

spans.text: participants were instructed to view the depicted emotional scenes as parts of a movie clip or TV show that displayed fake or artificially set-up situations created to give rise to emotions.

description.value: Expressive suppression condition. Participants watched emotional pictures as in the natural condition but were instructed not to display felt emotions externally, including through breathing, heart rate, skin conductance, or facial expression, then rated the feeling evoked.

spans.text: the participants were told to watch the pictures similarly to the NAT condition, but with the important difference that they were instructed not to display any felt emotions that could become visible on the outside

instructions.value: Participants viewed emotional pictures under three instructions: natural viewing, imagining the scenes as real situations; cognitive reappraisal, viewing the scenes as fake or artificially staged movie or television situations; and expressive suppression, viewing the scenes as real while suppressing any outward emotional expressions. In the baseline condition, participants judged photographic quality. After each image, they rated their feeling from very negative to very positive on a four-point scale.
